objetivo.en: Greet people according to the time of day and ask how they are, with tú or usted.

nota.en: The h is silent: “OH-lah”.
From waking up until about noon.
From noon until it gets dark.
After dark, to say hello or goodbye.
Informal: with friends and people your age.
For a woman, with or without her name: la señora Rosa.
don Jorge = Mr. Jorge. For a woman: doña.

explicacion.en: Días is masculine: buenos días. Tardes and noches are feminine: buenas tardes, buenas noches.
With an older person or someone you don't know well, use usted: ¿Cómo está? Use ¿cómo estás? only with a friend or someone your age.
Noches is feminine, so the greeting is buenas noches, not buenos.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the five vowels

texto.en: Spanish has only five vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and each one always sounds the same: short, clear and pure. Unlike English, a Spanish vowel never glides into a second sound: say “o”, not “o-u” as in go. a is like the a in father, but shorter; e is like the e in bed; i is like the ee in see, but short; o is a short, round “oh”; u is like the oo in rule, but short. Say them slowly: buenas, buenos, noches, días, gracias.

titulo.en: Greeting by the time of day, with tú or usted

texto.en: Spanish greets by time of day: buenos días until about noon, buenas tardes from noon until it gets dark, and buenas noches after dark. Buenas noches works both to say hello and to say goodbye at night, so it covers both “good evening” and “good night”. Note that días is masculine (buenos días) while tardes and noches are feminine. Hola works at any time of day, especially with friends and people your age. To ask how someone is, use ¿Qué tal? or ¿Cómo estás? with friends and people your age (tú), and ¿Cómo está? with older people and people you don't know well (usted). You can answer bien, muy bien or más o menos, and give the question back with ¿Y tú? or ¿Y usted? In Ecuador, don and doña before a first name show respect: don Jorge. Emma uses usted with señora Rosa and don Jorge, and tú with Daniela.

objetivo.en: Say goodbye according to when you will see the person again: chao, hasta luego, hasta mañana, nos vemos.

nota.en: From Italian ciao; very common in Latin America.
More formal; it doesn't say when you will meet again.
You can add a time: nos vemos mañana.

explicacion.en: Hola is for arriving. To leave, use chao, hasta luego or hasta mañana.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Hasta mañana, Daniela. (you will see her tonight at home)

explicacion.en: Hasta mañana is only for tomorrow. If you will see the person later today, say hasta luego or nos vemos.

explicacion.en: Adiós sounds final. With a friend you will see soon, say chao, hasta luego or hasta mañana.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the silent h

texto.en: In Spanish the letter h is always silent: hola sounds like “OH-lah”, hasta like “AH-stah”, and hasta luego like “AH-stah LWEH-go”. Don't pronounce it like the English h in hello. Also remember that ch, as in chao, sounds like the ch in chair.

titulo.en: Saying goodbye: when will you see each other?

texto.en: In Spanish you choose your goodbye by when you will see the person again. Chao is informal and friendly, from Italian ciao. Adiós is more formal and doesn't say when you will meet again, so it can sound final; with a friend you'll see soon, prefer chao or hasta + a moment. Hasta luego means “see you later” and hasta mañana means “see you tomorrow”; you can also say hasta el lunes (until Monday). Nos vemos is “see you around” and you can add a time: nos vemos mañana, nos vemos más tarde. Buenas noches also works as a goodbye at night. Compare English: “see you later” and “see you tomorrow” are the same idea, but Spanish builds them with hasta, which literally means “until”.

objetivo.en: Say what your name is, ask someone else's name with tú or usted, and say what other people are called.

explicacion.en: Llamarse needs its pronoun: me llamo. Spanish says literally “I call myself Emma”.
The verb ending must match the person: tú → te llamas, usted → se llama.
Don't drop the se: ella se llama Daniela.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: ll and y

texto.en: In Latin America the letters ll and y sound the same, like the y in yes: llamo, llamas, yo, ella. Say them with a clear, short “yah”: ya, ye, yi, yo, yu. The two l's in ll are one single sound, not the “l-l” of English.

titulo.en: Saying and asking names with llamarse

texto.en: To give your name, Spanish says literally “I call myself”: me llamo Emma. The little word before the verb changes with the person: me llamo (yo), te llamas (tú), se llama (él, ella, usted), nos llamamos (nosotros) and se llaman (ellos, ellas, ustedes). Notice that se llama (one person) and se llaman (two or more) share the same se: only the -n at the end shows that there is more than one person. Ask with ¿Cómo te llamas? for a friend or someone your age (tú), and ¿Cómo se llama usted? for an older person or a stranger (usted). Compare English: “My name is Emma” becomes me llamo Emma, not “yo llamo Emma”. For more than one person, Latin America uses ustedes (you all): se llaman.

objetivo.en: Say what nationality you are and what nationality other people are, using the correct masculine or feminine form.

nota.en: Same form for men and women.
No capital letter; the accent mark goes away in the feminine.
The ñ sounds like “ny”.

explicacion.en: The nationality matches the person: -o for a man, -a for a woman. Daniela is a woman: ecuatoriana.
After a consonant, add -a for a woman: inglés → inglesa (the accent mark disappears).
Estadounidense ends in -e and is the same for men and women: no -a.
In Spanish, nationalities are not capitalized.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the letter ñ

texto.en: The letter ñ (eñe) sounds like the ni in onion: español, española. It is a different letter from n. Practice: español, española, año (year), niño (child).

Nationalities in Spanish are adjectives and agree with the person: -o for men and -a for women (ecuatoriano, ecuatoriana; mexicano, mexicana). If the masculine ends in a consonant, add -a for women: inglés → inglesa (the accent mark goes away) and español → española. Some forms are the same for men and women, like estadounidense. English does not change its word (an American man, an American woman), so watch the ending. Use soy, eres or es: soy estadounidense, Andrés es ecuatoriano. Spanish does not use a before the nationality (not “soy un estadounidense”) and does not capitalize it. To say where you are from, use ser de + city: soy de Chicago, es de Quito.

nota.en: The same for men and women.

nota.en: Don't forget the a before a person.
The letter r is called erre (some people say ere); rr is doble erre.
The feminine of don.

explicacion.en: Before a person you need a: te presento a Daniela.

explicacion.en: With an older person, use usted: le presento a…

titulo.en: Sound of the day: r and rr

texto.en: Spanish has two r sounds. A single r between vowels is a quick tap, like the tt in butter said fast (American English): pero, ere. The rr is a strong, rolled sound: perro, erre. At the start of a word, a single r also sounds like the strong rr: Rosa, rápido. The double letter rr is one sound written with two letters, like ll. Practice: pero, perro, Rosa.

titulo.en: Spelling a name and making introductions

texto.en: To ask how a word is written, say ¿Cómo se escribe? and answer with the names of the letters: García is ge, a, erre, ce, i con tilde, a. The letters ll and rr are two letters but one sound, called doble ele and doble erre. Introduce someone with te presento a… (tú: friends, people your age) or le presento a… (usted: older people, formal), and always put a before the person: te presento a Daniela. The answer is mucho gusto, or encantado (a man) / encantada (a woman), and the other person says igualmente. In Ecuador, women and mixed pairs often greet with a kiss on the cheek, and two men shake hands.
